facts.claim: Ben Folds wrote the song. It was the lead single from his third solo album, Way to Normal (2008), and it features Regina Spektor on duet vocals.
Way to Normal was produced by Dennis Herring. It was recorded at Folds' own studio in Nashville, and Herring's earlier credits include Elvis Costello, The Hives and Modest Mouse.
Folds' regular bassist Jared Reynolds and drummer Sam Smith joined him on the album.
Producer Dennis Herring is credited with drums on 'You Don't Know Me' (credited as 'Drumming With Knobs'). Spektor is credited with guest vocals.
Spektor's guest vocal was recorded at Avatar Studios in New York. The album was mixed at Quad Studio in New York and mastered at Masterdisk in New York. Spektor appears courtesy of Sire/Warner Bros.
Folds told Rolling Stone it was simple: he called Spektor up and they went and did it. He had a part in mind for her, but she added a lot that wasn't planned, which he liked.

The video was directed by comedy duo Tim Heidecker and Eric Wareheim, who play an unhappy couple. Folds, Sam Smith and Jared Reynolds play on the lawn outside their house, and Spektor does not appear.
PopMatters describes the song as Folds and Spektor trading lines in the chorus while Folds wonders in the verse what is keeping the couple together.
Folds wrote part of the album as he finalized a two-year divorce. He said the songs are not topical and that the record is about being free.
Before the release, Folds leaked fake versions of six songs, recorded in an eight-hour Dublin session. Friends bundled them with the real singles, including 'You Don't Know Me'.

research.lineage: A piano-driven, lyric-focused singer-songwriter pop/rock song in the tradition of Folds' Ben Folds Five work, paired with a guest from the indie/anti-folk scene.

draft:
Two people sing **You Don't Know Me** at each other, and the only thing they agree on is the chorus. Ben Folds and Regina Spektor trade the title line back and forth, often landing in unison or parallel thirds. So the harmony is doing something sly: two voices, perfectly matched, each accusing the other of never having listened. It's the most together this couple gets.

Folds wrote it, and the verse is his slow-dawning question. How can two people share a life "for so long" and never know what's going on in each other's heads? The images get sharper as the resentment builds. He pictures himself propped up like a mannequin or a cardboard stand-up, painted with whatever face the other person wanted. Then comes the line where the song stops being a gripe and turns on both of them: "It was we who were the cliché." He doesn't let himself off. They saw the couple in the coma and recognized themselves, and they "carried on anyway."

The bridge is where the feeling cracks open. Folds runs through the version of himself he thinks his partner holds, a clueless chump, an errant dog who needs a shorter leash, and then blurts the question underneath all of it: "Why the fuck would you want me back?" It's anger, but it's also hurt and a little pleading. The answer he offers himself, that maybe it's *because* she doesn't know him, is the bleakest joke in the song. Then the confession stalls. He can't get it out the way he means it, "'Cause I know you'll only change it," and the lyric gives up on words entirely, dissolving into a run of wordless ahs.

The sound keeps all this moving instead of sinking. A driving, arpeggiated piano figure with a strong bass line and a slight swing carries it at a moderate clip. Folds sings clear and a little nasal, conversational, like he's arguing across a kitchen table. Spektor's voice is breathier and sits higher, and her echoes ("What?") land like interruptions. Folds said he called her up with a part in mind, and she added a lot he hadn't planned, which he liked. You can hear it in the way her asides poke holes in his speeches.

This is classic Folds, the piano-pop of his Ben Folds Five years, smart-mouthed and melodic, pulled toward the anti-folk side by his guest. He made the album, produced by Dennis Herring, while finalizing a two-year divorce, though he insisted the songs weren't topical and that the record was about being free. Fair enough. This one doesn't sound free yet. It sounds like the moment right before.

It sticks because the bounce lets you sing along to an argument nobody wins, and by the last chorus you're not sure which side you're on.
